entries.text: NOTE ECDOTIQUE ET MÉCANIQUE [F] — RECONSTRUCTIONS. Lorsque la syntaxe latine autorise plusieurs dispositions matérielles, l’édition ne choisit pas silencieusement une reconstruction. L’ambiguïté du texte est conservée ; les hypothèses graphiques sont signalées et justifiées en note.

entries.label: APPARAT CRITIQUE
entries.text: APPARAT CRITIQUE ET INTERPRÉTATIF — X.16. La hauteur de l’hélépole d’Épimachos est corrigée à CXXXV pieds selon la constitution critique moderne, contre CXXV dans une partie de la tradition. L’épisode de Callias et Diognète sert en outre de réflexion sur l’échelle : une maquette peut paraître viable et échouer lorsqu’on l’agrandit. Vitruve formule ainsi, au moyen d’exemples mécaniques, une mise en garde contre le passage linéaire et naïf du modèle réduit à l’ouvrage réel. SYNTHÈSE POUR LES ARCHITECTES [T] — CLÔTURE DU LIVRE X. Le dénouement déplace l’attention de la machine isolée vers le projet adaptatif. Défense, terrain, eau, matériaux, échelle, information et décision tactique se combinent selon les circonstances. Le principe final est méthodologique : aucun catalogue ne remplace le jugement de l’architecte lorsque changent l’échelle, le site et les conditions d’usage. 30

entries.label: APPARAT CRITIQUE COMPARATIF
entries.text: APPARAT CRITIQUE COMPARATIF [F] — X.16. La clôture du traité oppose machines offensives et ressources défensives à travers des exempla d’ingéniosité, de ruse technique et d’adaptation au site. Le caractère narratif de ces épisodes est conservé sans les transformer en prescriptions militaires modernes. SYNTHÈSE ECDOTIQUE — CLÔTURE DU LIVRE X. La révision de X est complète, de machina et des systèmes de levage à l’hydraulique, l’artillerie et la poliorcétique. Les zones de risque maximal sont identifiées : nombres, fractions, suppléments, vocabulaire grec, noms de pièces et reconstructions dépendantes des figures. SYNTHÈSE POUR LES ARCHITECTES [T] — LIVRE X. Vitruve réunit statique pratique, transmission du mouvement, hydraulique, instrumentation, torsion et construction de grands dispositifs dans la discipline de l’architectus. L’édition maintient distincts texte antique, explication mécanique et formalisation ingénierique moderne. Status textus X. V521 a déclaré achevée la collatio directe continue de H pour le Livre X (ff. 139r–161v) ; la révision V548 (T.13bb) et la nouvelle collation de V552 (T.13ff), complétée par le f. 155v dans V553, la remplacent. La passe de X.1–X.9 confirme notamment que H ne transmet pas ⟨est, cum⟩en X.1.1 ; transmet la séquence défective ad apparatus spectatione et ne marque matériellement aucune lacune après quinque etiam stellarum natura en X.1.4 ;

entries.label: Note comparative
entries.text: Note comparative [F] — Livre 1.2.1 (les six principes). La liste fondamentale — ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, distributio — est parmi les passages les plus débattus, en raison du poids technique des termes grecs que Vitruve juxtapose. Les éditions de référence s’accordent sur la conservation des termes grecs et diffèrent sur leurs nuances : Granger (Loeb, 1931) les traduit par des équivalents fixes ; Rowland et Howe (Cambridge, 1999) insistent sur le sens dela conception(dispositioet ses ideae) ;l’équipeBudé (dir.Gros) analyse l’influencede la technè et de la rhétorique hellénistiques ; Corso et Romano (Einaudi) développent le commentaireterminologique.Cetteéditionconservelejumelagelatin-grecettraduitenutilisantsa propre terminologie, sans adopter de version étrangère. [Note historico-architecturale] Parmi les six principes, symmetria et eurythmia régissent la proportion ; ordinatio et distributio, mesure et économie ; decor, adéquation ; et dispositio présentent les trois ideae —ichnographia (plan),orthographia(élévation)etscaenographia(perspective)—,laracinedelareprésentation architecturale moderne. 1.3.2 « haec autem ita fieri debent ut habeatur ratio firmitatis, utilitatis, venustatis » — « ces principes doivent être mis en œuvre en tenant compte de la solidité, de l’utilité et de la beauté ». Collation : Rose 1899 ; Gros (Budé I) ; cf. Rowland-Howe, c

entries.label: Note comparative
entries.text: Note comparative [F] — Lib. 4.1.9–10 (κατατηξίτεχνος). L’épithète que les Athéniens donnaient à Callimaque est un terme à la signification controversée : composé de κατατήκω (« fondre, consumer ») et de τέχνη (« art »), il admet deux interprétations : « celui qui affine ou perfectionne l’art », éloge d’une finition extrême, ou, avec une nuance ironique, « celui qui est consumé par l’art », poussant le propos jusqu’à l’affectation. Les éditions le reflètent

entries.label: Note terminologique
entries.text: Note terminologique : Alors que les versions modernes privilégient des équivalents fonctionnels (Granger emploie « commodity » au lieu d’« utilitas ») et que les versions françaises classiques adaptent les termes (Perrault), cette édition conserve la racine latine et y ajoute une précision technique visant à restituer la nuance architecturale. La symmetria est ici traitée comme une proportion commensurable et non comme la « symétrie » (spéculaire) moderne ; le décor est conservé sous le terme de decorum, en raison de sa connotation éthico-esthétique de « ce qui est approprié » ; et la distributio est distinguée de la dispositio, car chez Vitruve, elle concerne la gestion des matériaux, des coûts et du contexte social plutôt que l’agencement spatial.

entries.label: Critical apparatus
entries.text: Critical apparatus: Restitution and academic writing (The Enlightened and Academic Reception) “The process of exegesis and visual fixation of the Vitruvian treatise reached its critical and institutional maturity during the centuries of the Enlightenment 195

entries.label: CRITICAL NOTE
entries.text: CRITICAL NOTE — I.1.1. The manuscript tradition and modern editions do not agree on every detail of this definition. This edition retains cuius iudicio probantur omnia, a transmitted reading also adopted in the modern critical text consulted; Granger, by contrast, regarded the clause as a possible interpolation and proposed different punctuation. For fabrica, the readings perficit[ur] and opus [est] retain editorial brackets. The concluding phrase is given as sollertiae ac rationis 106 cuius iudicio probantur omnia] A disputed passage in the editorial tradition. Krohn (1912) prints these words in the text; other editions have marked them as doubtful or enclosed them in brackets. This edition retains them, but records the discussion without attributing a deletion to the manuscript tradition where the apparatus for the passage has not been verified. 214

entries.label: TEXTUAL NOTE
entries.text: TEXTUAL NOTE — I.1.3. THE ADOPTED TEXT RETAINS PERITUS graphidos, the reading printed in the modern critical editions consulted. Since this edition offers no new recensio, variants are not attributed here to particular manuscripts, nor are formulas such as “codd.” reproduced without direct verification in an identifiable critical apparatus. He must therefore be literate, skilled in drawing and trained in geometry; he must know historical narratives, have listened attentively to philosophers, understand music, possess some knowledge of medicine, be acquainted with the opinions of jurists, and understand astronomy and the workings of the heavens. Critical Apparatus • Tum maxime etiam in architectura] “Above all also in architecture”. Etiam is retained in the Spanish edition and Krohn’s text; no omission of etiam is adopted without a documented manuscript witness. • haec duo insunt: quod significatur et quod significat] Vitruvius distinguishes the subject or matter under discussion from its demonstrative explanation through the principles of the disciplines. This is a semantic explanation, not a claim of manuscript unanimity. • docilem] The word denotes a disposition or capacity to learn. No particular textual judgment is added where a relevant variant has not been documented. The Spanish edition heads this lexical note ingenio et disciplinae docilem; the running text has ad disci

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.4–5.5 (echea). In the Budé, Book V is the work of Catherine Saliou (2009), whose commentary on the theater and its acoustics is standard. In the Cambridge commentary, Thomas N. Howe observes that Vitruvius here singles out an uncommon Greek technical feature, for which only between eight and sixteen possible sites are known. Granger (Loeb) preserves the Greek musical terminology (nete, paramese, mese, hypate); Corso– Romano and Tavernor–Schofield accompany the passage with diagrams of the scale. In 5.5 the manuscript tradition presents a crux (diatessaron for diapente in the series of intervals), discussed since Rose; this edition follows Rose's text and translates in its own voice. Nor could anyone build hydraulic machines or other instruments similar to these organs without knowing the principles of music. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius continues to justify the need for musical knowledge for the architect, now moving from the military field to the acoustic - architectural field. Key points: 1. Theater acoustics: Vitruvius describes one of the most sophisticated acoustic systems of Antiquity: the echeia, or bronze resonating vessels. These 234

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.2.2. Krohn marks [modica] and [commoditas] as doubtful in the definition of ordinatio. This edition keeps them visibly marked wherever they occur in the adopted critical text and avoids building on them a doctrine dependent on their authenticity. Transmitted wording, editorial deletion, and supplementation are distinct philological categories and must be identified separately. Terminological note. Ordinatio cannot be equated without qualification with modern “order”, nor dispositio with ordinary “arrangement”. In this context, ordinatio concerns modulation and the correspondence of parts; dispositio concerns their concrete ordering and the modes of representing the project. The Greek terms τάξις, διάθεσις, ποσότης and ἰδέαι are retained because they contribute to Vitruvius’s conceptual precision. Exegesis Notes 1. The Ontology of Design: The Verb Constat: Vitruvius does not use the verbs habere (to have) or comprehendere (to understand). The use of constat ex implies that architecture emerges and subsists only when these six principles coexist simultaneously. If even one of them is missing, the constructed object ceases to be architecture (architecture) and degrades to a mere utilitarian building (fabrica). This nuance is important: the six principles are not optional tools, but rather the formal and efficient causes of sacred and civil space. 2. Vitruvius’s Gr

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.2.9. The adopted text follows the reference reading used in this edition: et ad pecuniae copiam, aedificia apte disponentur and the rest of the sequence as printed in Krohn. Generic manuscript attributions and variants from early editions are not retained here unless checked directly in an identifiable critical apparatus. Distributionis] Genitive of distributio: the passage introduces its second aspect, the arrangement of buildings for different uses. Aedificia apte disponentur] “Buildings will be suitably arranged”. The adopted phrase concerns planning for intended use and the occupants’ circumstances. Patrum familiarum] “Heads of households” or “householders”. The wording belongs to the comparison of buildings appropriate to different owners. Pecuniae copiam] “Available financial means”. The genitive pecuniae depends on copiam in the adopted text. Eloquentiae dignitatem] “The standing or dignity of eloquence”. It characterizes the needs of advocates in the passage’s social comparison. Constitui videtur] “It appears to be determined”. The adopted construction forms part of the conclusion on distribution. Influunt] “Flow in”. The term describes the public business and consultations that come to the houses of leading citizens. 274

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.3.1. The Latin text is checked against Rose and Krohn. This edition does not seek to establish a new recensio; its observations are therefore confined to problems affecting translation or interpretation and avoid unverified manuscript attributions. Terminological note — I.3.1. Aedificatio, gnomonice and machinatio are the three parts of architectura according to this chapter. Machinatio denotes the theory and practice of machines; gnomonice, astronomical and time measurement by shadows. Machinatio should not automatically be translated as “engineering”, nor gnomonice as “astronomy”, since both equivalents enlarge the scope of the ancient terms. 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.3.1. For the fixation of the Latin text, compare the archetypal edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 11-12; and the critical reading of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 12. • machinatio: The traditional translation of " engineering " is amended to " mechanical". In the context of the 1st century BC, machinatio strictly refers to the science of machines (both civil traction and military poliorctics), differentiating itself from the contemporary and institutionalized meaning of general engineering. • explicatio: The term is more precisely cast as "layout " or "deployment" of private b

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 1.3.2 (firmitas · utilitas · venustas). The canonical triad of a building's qualities. The major editions render it 279

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.3.2. The text is checked against Rose and Krohn. The adopted reading retains emendata et sine inpeditione usus locorum dispositio and apta et commoda distributio. This edition reproduces minor variants only when they affect the translated meaning. 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.3.2. For the textual fixation, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 12; and the revision of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 12. • habeatur ratio: It is translated with greater academic precision as " take into account" or "attend to", maintaining the structure of the technical conditional of the treatise. • ad solidum depressio: the foundations are to be excavated down to firm bearing ground. Solidum denotes a sufficiently stable stratum; it does not require bedrock in every case. The passage concerns the support of the foundations, not the sinking of a finished building. • Diligent selection of resources without avarice. The Latin excludes avaricious parsimony in the procurement of resources.It alludes to the sources of resources or supplies of materials available in the area. The expression sine avaritia means literally "without stinginess" or "without parsimony", implying that a poorly understood economy harms the structure. 280

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.4.5. The adopted text transmits στοιχεῖα, “elements” or “principles”. This edition retains the reading and confines its commentary to its role in Vitruvius’s argument, without reconstructing a history of manuscript corruption that has not been checked directly against the witnesses. 1.4.7 Sed si qui voluerit diligentius haec sensu percipere, animadvertat attendatque naturas avium et piscium et terrestrium animalium, et ita 292

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.4.10. The authorial Spanish base marks a lacuna after the cattle near Knossos, as does the adopted Krohn text. The electronic transcription of Rose supplies <lienosa> sunt, “have diseased spleens”, to complete the contrast with Gortyna. This is an editorial supplement, not a directly verified reading of Harley or Cotton. Asplenon (ἄσπληνον) is the plant name in the adopted text; its usual comparison with spleenwort belongs to botanical interpretation, not to the constitution of the damaged clause.

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.4.10. Krohn’s critical text retains a lacuna after proxime Gnoson; an unverified conjecture is therefore not introduced into the Latin as though it were transmitted text. Ἄσπληνον is the plant’s Greek name in the passage; this edition does not impose a single modern botanical identification. 300

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Inspection of viscera. The use of sacrificed animals to assess the healthiness of pastures and waters is retained as an ancient practice described by Vitruvius. It is neither recast as a modern diagnostic method nor omitted because it lies outside present architectural practice. 307

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.6.3. Rose (1899, 23) prints the restoration <igitur venti si ex habitationibus> at the opening of the section; Krohn (1912, 21) prints <Venti autem si ex habitationibus>. The Spanish note states that Rose’s restoration is adopted, but the Spanish edition’s running Latin follows the latter wording. The text printed here follows the authorial Spanish edition’s running Latin and records the editorial difference. Editorial unanimity must not be asserted where reconstructions of the lacuna differ. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 3. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.6.3. For the philological analysis of Aeolian medical terminology and the gaps in the main manuscripts, see Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 21-22; and Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 21-22. • Medicinae contrariae / temperaturam: Vitruvius adopts the postulates of the Hippocratic treatise On Airs, Waters, and Places. Temperature in Vitruvian Latin is not the modern quantitative measurement, but the notion of climatic equilibrium and proportion. If the urban fabric slows down air currents, a protected microclimate is generated that optimizes bodily homeostasis. • Gravedo, arteriace...: Ancient symptomatology of respiratory ailments. Gravedo defines heavy nasal congestion or coryza; arteriace is a medic

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.6.9. Rose’s text (1899) retains the figure in numerals with a supralinear bar; the translation expands it as 31,500,000 paces. The edition retains the reference to Eratosthenes without reconstructing here his complete historical method of measurement or imposing a single modern value for the ancient stadium. Academic translation 1.6.9 Those who know a vast number of wind names may be surprised that we have stated that there are only eight. However, if they take into consideration 129 Eratosthenes of Cyrene (Greek Ἐρατοσθένης; born between 276 and 273 BC at Cyrene, died around 194 BC at Alexandria) was an exceptionally versatile Greek scholar at the height of Hellenistic science. 130 Vitruvius attributes a circumference of 252,000 stadia for the Earth to Eratosthenes. Conversion into modern units depends on the length assigned to the stadium; the edition therefore retains the ancient value without imposing a single equivalent. 345

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.6.13. Rose (1899, 29–30) and Krohn (1912, 25–26) print G–H in the southern sector and I–K in the northern sector; both retain lineae decussatim for M–O and L–N, and the final phrase gnomon ponatur. In the M –O/L–N instruction, the Latin reads lineae decussatim, followed later by gnomon ponatur; per centrum and linea ponatur are not the corresponding readings there. Per centrum remains correct in the preceding G–K/H–I instruction: the two constructions must not be conflated. Academic translation 1.6.13 Next, a measurement equal to one sixteenth of the total perimeter of the circumference will be taken with the compass. Placing the point of the compass on the meridian line, just where it intersects the circle at the southern end — marked with the letter E —, two marks will be made to the right and left, where the letters G and H will be placed respectively. Similarly, at the northernmost point — marked with the letter F — the compass point will be placed, and marks will be made to the right and left where the letters I and K will be located. Following this, straight lines will be drawn passing through the center: one from G to K and another from H to I. In this way, the space between G and H will constitute the sector assigned to the Austro (South) wind, and the space between I and K will correspond to the Septentrio (North). The remaining areas — three to the ri

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Secuntur and sequuntur. The spelling variation does not alter the meaning of sequor. The edition adopts sequuntur in its normalized text. The printed apparatuses of Krohn (1912, 20, line 7) and Rose (1899, 22, line 5) report secuntur for H, which their lists identify as Harley MS 2767. This is an indirect attribution from the editors’ apparatuses, not a claim to direct inspection of the manuscript folio. The variation is orthographic, not semantic. Urban note — Winds. The principle of disrupting the wind’s direct entry can be compared with bioclimatic strategies for urban layout, but the physiological theory of healthy or harmful winds belongs to the ancient medical setting. The edition keeps the two levels distinct. 5. Rowland and Howe, Vitruvius, 31. Critical Interlineation 358

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — I.7.2. Krohn’s text (1912) is followed: quo ⟨non quolibet⟩ nomine semper homines…; cum religione…; and de earum symmetriis, with ⟨deinde⟩ as an editorial supplement. Rose (1899) prints a different text here— quo non omnes semper homines…; cum religiose…. The difference is recorded because it affects the wording, although it does not alter the passage’s general meaning. 364

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — II.5.2–3. The Spanish edition follows the sequence printed by Krohn (1912, 37): the weight-loss sentence stands parenthetically at the opening of II.5.3, before the account of immersion, latent heat and the absorption of sand. Rose (1899, 40–41) places the immersion account before the weight-loss sentence. Both accounts are retained here, with the running text and translation ordered according to the authorial Spanish edition. In the phrase concerning latent heat, Krohn prints prius quem ex ignis vi recepit, “which it had previously received from the force of the fire”. the Spanish edition’s translation “antes de recibir la fuerza del fuego” reverses that temporal relation; the English follows 416

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Book II. The Latin is checked against Krohn (1912). Material names, construction procedures, ancient units and the distinction between Vitruvius’s physical explanation and modern materials science are retained. Orthographical variation, editorial supplementation and substantive readings are treated separately; the antiquity of a practice does not establish the precise date of a surviving archaeological example. 462

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — III.1.3. The adopted text reads item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus, followed by namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus. These words describe the navel as the center of the circle traced around the outstretched body. No specific reading of Harley MS 2767 is established by this note. The relation to Leonardo’s drawing, made around 1490 and now in the Gallerie dell’Accademia in Venice, belongs to the history of the passage’s reception. Possible routes through the printed edition associated with Sulpicius or through Francesco di Giorgio Martini require separate historical documentation. See Vitruvius, De architectura 3.1.3; Martin Kemp, Leonardo da Vinci: The Marvellous Works of Nature and Man (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006), 96–99.

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — III.1.3. Krohn’s text gives “item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus. namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus…”. There is therefore no basis for treating namque as a corruption or dittography. The passage describes, successively, the relation of the body to a circumference centered on the navel and the equality between bodily height and arm-span that permits comparison with a square. Renaissance reception, above all Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing now known as Vitruvian Man, belongs to the history of reception and must be distinguished from establishing the Latin text.

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 3.1.2–3 (homo ad circulum et quadratum). The treatise's most celebrated passage: the well-proportioned body, laid out with limbs extended, inscribed—with its center at the navel (umbilicus)—in the circle drawn with a compass (circinus) and, at once, in the square. Text and commentary should be distinguished: the adopted text speaks of a «homo bene figuratus», without the formula «ad circulum et quadratum», which is a fixture of the editorial tradition (see the critical note to 3.1.3). The reference editions 471

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — III.1.2–3. Vitruvius takes the homo bene figuratus as a comparison for architectural commensurability. The Latin text does not contain the formula homo ad circulum et quadratum: this is a later historiographical designation. Nor does it state that circle and square must share the same geometrical center. The navel is the center of the circumference described by the outstretched limbs; comparison with the square, by contrast, proceeds from the equality of height and arm-span. Architectural and philological note — Homo bene figuratus. The human body serves as an analogy of commensurability: each member has a ratio to the whole. The text does not prescribe that temples should literally reproduce a human figure, nor does it contain the modern expression “Vitruvian Man”. Graphic reconstructions of circle and square belong to the history of reception and must be labeled accordingly. 4. ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem. igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, <> maxime in aedibus deorum, <⟨quod eorum⟩> operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere. Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members answer

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — III.1.5–6. The discussion of six, ten and their proportional fractions is retained in full according to the authorial Spanish edition and Krohn (1912, 60–61). Krohn marks ab palmo pes for deletion in III.1.5 and supplies ⟨X⟩ before singularibus rebus; Rose (1899, 65) prints ab palmo pes without those deletion brackets. In III.1.6 Rose (1899, 66) prints a bracketed section from bessem through διπλάσιον, and his apparatus describes it as an interpolation from an ancient mathematical book. Krohn does not enclose the corresponding numerical excursus in those brackets. Rose’s assessment is thus documented as his editorial judgment; it is not evidence of an independently inspected manuscript omission. Latin fractional terminology and Greek names of ratios are retained, since the two systems must not be collapsed into an unsupported modern equivalence.

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — III.1.6. The excursus on six and numerical ratios is retained in Krohn’s text. This edition will not call it an interpolation or a spurious passage without expressly documenting a decision in the critical apparatus of the edition cited. The terminology combines Latin fractions with Greek proportional vocabulary; the Greek terms are therefore retained where a single modern equivalent would be reductive. 474

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — III.2.5–6. Krohn (1912, 63), followed by the authorial Spanish edition, transposes sine postico before the examples beginning in porticu Metelli; Rose (1899, 68) places it after Honoris et Virtutis. The different scope is preserved in the adopted translation rather than silently settled by an archaeological identification. In III.2.6 Krohn prints Hermogenis Alabandei, identifying Hermogenes as Alabandean; Rose prints Hermogenis, Alabandis etiam Apollinis, locating the temple of Apollo at Alabanda. The Spanish edition follows Krohn. Menesthes is the named architect of Apollo’s temple, not Hermogenes. These are differences in editorial constitution and punctuation, not newly collated manuscript readings. 7. dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a Chersiphrone constituta. 480

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — III.3.1, 5 and 9. The two Spanish formulations in the Spanish edition do not distribute the qualification “farther apart than is fitting” in the same way. Its running Latin and first translation follow Krohn (1912, 64), attaching amplius quam oportet inter se diductis to diastylos. Rose (1899, 69) instead attaches rarius quam oportet inter se diductis to araeostylos; the Spanish edition’s explanatory parallel follows this latter distribution. The English preserves both authorial paragraphs separately and records the difference, rather than merging the two editorial constitutions. The varicae restored in III.3.5 follows Krohn (1912, 65), whose apparatus attributes the reading to Turnebus; ⟨improviso⟩ in III.3.9 is marked as Krohn’s supplement (1912, 66). Both belong to the authorial Spanish edition’s adopted constitution and are not presented as newly verified manuscript words. 2. ergo pycnostylos est cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae. item systylos est in qua duarum columnarum crassitudo in intercolumnio poterit conlocari, et spirarum plinthides aeque magnae sint ei spatio quod fuerit inter duas plinthides, quemadmodum est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae. 483

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — III.3.8. the Spanish edition’s running Latin and Krohn’s printed text (1912, 66, line 4) give XXXIV, thirty-four; Rose’s printed text (1899, 71, line 13) gives XXXVIII, thirty-eight. Krohn’s apparatus explicitly records “xxxiv Phil: xxxviii x”, identifying thirty-four as the editorial reading associated with Philander and distinguishing it from the reading labeled x. This confirms the choice of thirty-four in the authorial base and corrects the Spanish comparative note’s attribution of thirty-eight to the current Perseus text of Krohn. Neither H nor Cotton is independently assigned a reading here. Hermogenes’s association with the pseudodipteral scheme belongs to Vitruvius’s own account. 9. Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo est inventa, ut aspectus propter asperitatem intercolumniorum habeat auctoritatem, praeterea, si ex ⟨improviso⟩ imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum laxamento liberam moram. Haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris aedium dispositionibus! Quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum Hermogenes fecisse reliquisseque fontes, unde posteri possent haurire disciplinarum rationes. For the principle of the pteroma and the arrangement of columns about the temple was devised so that the appearance might have dignity through the relief creat

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 3.3.13 (entasis). The entasis (ἔντασις)—the slight swelling or adiectio of the shaft that corrects the optical illusion of concavity—is, with the contractions and the inclination of the members, one of the system's optical «temperings». Vitruvius defers its drawing to a plate «at the end of the book» (in extremo libro), lost in the manuscript tradition, which has made the exact profile an open problem since the Renaissance (Fra Giocondo, Alberti, the practice of the curves). The editions reflect this: Rose (Teubner, 1899) fixes the text without restoring the figure; Granger (Loeb, 1931) renders adiectio as the «increase» of the shaft; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) discuss the geometric reconstruction of the curve; the Budé (dir. Gros) reviews the hypotheses of the profile (parabola, arc of a circle). The present edition keeps the term and translates in its own words, adopting no external version. [Historical-architectural note] The entasis is the most celebrated of the Greek optical corrections; the Parthenon combines it with the curvature of the stylobate (see scamilli impares, 3.4.5). 491

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — III.3.13. Ἔντασις denotes the addition to or modification of the shaft’s profile in its middle region. The surviving text refers to a forma et ratio at the end of the book; the loss or incomplete transmission of the figures prevents turning that reference into a single geometrical reconstruction. The edition therefore retains the Greek term and distinguishes textual testimony from the various reconstructions proposed since the Renaissance. Technical note — Rhythm and module. The eustyle is not merely the “ideal type”: Vitruvius presents it as a solution balancing usus, species and firmitas through ordinary intercolumniations of two and a quarter diameters and a wider axial intercolumniation. A comparative table must show intercolumniation, diameter-to-height ratio and examples separately, avoiding confusion between measurements expressed in diameters and Roman feet. Metrological note — Doron. Vitruvius explains doron by reference to the palm and relates pentadoron/tetradoron to five/four palms. Any modern metric equivalent is given as an approximation dependent on the standard adopted; the ancient dimensions retain priority in the text. Construction note — Semilateria and joints. The alternation of lateres and semilateria is interpreted as a strategy for bonding facings and joints. Modern explanation of the bond is kept separate from Vitruvius’s exact words and

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — III.4.1. The Spanish edition follows Krohn (1912, 68) in reading ad solidum et in solido, “down to firm ground and into it”; Rose (1899, 73) prints ab solido et in solidum. The Spanish edition’s first rendering follows the former construction, while its parallel rendering begins “from firm ground and down to the firm”. Both authorial renderings are presented separately in English, with their different formulations visible. The adopted Latin follows the 494

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — III.4.4–5. The requirement for an odd number of steps, so that the ascent begins and ends with the right foot, and the riser limits of a dodrans and a dextans (¾ and ⅚ of a Roman foot) belong to III.4.4. They must be distinguished from scamilli impares in III.4.5. The latter phrase is associated with a central rise of the stylobate and an optical appearance of hollowing if it is set strictly level. Its precise material interpretation remains disputed; supports, offsets and unequal leveling elements are among the reconstructions proposed. The figure promised at the end of the book is not supplied by the surviving wording. Granger, Rowland and Howe, Gros, and Corso and Romano are relevant points of comparison for the reception of the problem; their individual solutions require direct consultation. The association with 497

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — Scamilli impares. The passage’s connection with the curvature or leveling of the stylobate and with optical corrections is plausible and forms part of its technical reception, but the exact material form of the scamilli has received divergent interpretations. Transmitted text, editorial conjecture and graphic reconstruction must remain typographically distinct. Comparative textual apparatus — III.4. The chapter combines foundations, stereobatae, stylobata, steps and podium with one of the most difficult passages of the technical tradition: “scamillos inpares”. The edition preserves the Latin phrase as a textual and architectural problem; it does not silently adopt a Renaissance or modern reconstruction as though it were the only possible reading. Metrological note — Steps and podium. Numbers of steps, heights and modular relationships are retained first in their ancient formulation. Any modern decimal or metric conversion is reserved for auxiliary tables; if a figure 498

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — III.5.3. The running Latin and the first Spanish rendering in the Spanish edition give the projection as an eighth plus a sixteenth of the column diameter. Its parallel Spanish rendering instead says “an eighth of the base, plus a sixteenth of the column diameter”. Both formulations are retained in separate English paragraphs. Krohn (1912, 70) and Rose (1899, 76) print proiectura erit spirae pars octava et sexta decuma pars crassitudinis columnae. The parallel version’s different explicit referent for the eighth is an authorial interpretation, not an independently established numerical manuscript variant. 4. Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam. Sic enim erunt figurae compositionis aedium contractura eius tali ratione exactae. When the bases have been completed and set in place, position the central columns of the pronaos and the rear part plumb through their central axes. The corner columns and those aligned with them along the temple’s right and left sides must have their inner faces, towards the cella walls, set vertically, while their

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Book III. The English translation derives from Diego Kurilo’s original Spanish text. Krohn’s Latin text and the electronic transcription of Rose provide independent controls for the passages discussed in this apparatus. The Book III edition established and translated by Pierre Gros (Budé, 1990) is an essential reference, but a complete independent collation of its critical apparatus is not claimed here. No individual manuscript reading or editorial decision is attributed to Gros, Rose, Krohn or Granger without identifiable documentary support. Greek ἀναλογία in III.1.1 is the adopted technical term; a damaged electronic transcription does not by itself demonstrate corruption in the manuscript tradition. Critical and comparative note — Conclusion of Book III. This edition’s checks distinguish three levels: (1) the adopted Latin text and its transmission problems; (2) the translation, which seeks to preserve technical terminology and argumentative syntax without introducing explanations foreign to the original; and (3) the historical and architectural commentary, where modern interpretations are recorded. The Latin has been systematically compared with Krohn (Teubner, 1912) in the passages reviewed. The Budé edition of Book III, established, translated and annotated by Pierre Gros (CUF, 1990), serves as a standard of philological and archaeological rigor and, w

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Numerals and fractions in III.5. Proportional sequences are passages at high risk of palaeographic and editorial corruption. The comparative apparatus therefore prioritizes discrepancies that alter a member’s module, height, projection or division; purely graphic or orthographic variants are not needlessly multiplied. Synthesis for architects — Book III. Vitruvius articulates the temple through relations between whole, members and module. The book’s contemporary value lies in understanding a historical system of dimensional coordination and visual correction, not in turning its proportions into universal standards. 513

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — IV, preface. Non ordinata sed incepta, uti particulas errabundas characterizes earlier architectural writings polemically as scattered and unfinished materials. The difficult syntax around ex tribus generibus and ionici generis moribus should not obscure the secure program: after the Ionic, Vitruvius will examine the Doric and Corinthian systems, their differences and properties. The transmitted wording, editorial constitution, ancient aetiology and modern archaeological assessment remain distinct levels of argument. 515

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 4.2 (structural truth). Here Vitruvius states one of the most influential doctrines of architectural theory: stone ornaments are the translation—petrification—of timber roofing (triglyphs from beam-ends, mutules from rafters, dentils from laths), so that they must not represent what cannot exist in constructional reality (quod non potest in veritate fieri… non… certam rationem habere). Hence his rejection of dentils beneath mutules. The editions fix the passage without major divergence (Rose, Teubner 1899; Budé, dir. Gros); Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress its scope as a principle of «constructional truth». [Historical-architectural note] It is the ancient root of modern structural rationalism: Laugier's «primitive hut» (Essai sur l'architecture, 1753), Viollet-le-Duc's rationalism, and, in the twentieth century, «truth to materials» and «form follows function». Cf. the note on the angular triglyph (4.3.1–2). 525

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — Bk. 4.3.1–2. The 'angular triglyph conflict' is the chief objection to the Doric in temples: the triglyph must fall at once over the column's axis and at the corner of the frieze—incompatible demands that force either the narrowing of the end intercolumniation or the distortion of the metope. Hence Arcesius, Pytheos, and Hermogenes rejected it. Vitruvius nonetheless sets out the corrected system. It is one of the classic problems of Greek architecture. Some ancient architects denied that sacred buildings should be built in the Doric style, because they created false and inappropriate symmetries. And so Arcesius denied it, Pythius as well, and Hermogenes no less. For when he had prepared a supply of marble for the completion of the Doric building, he changed it from the same supply and made it Ionic for the Free Father. However, it is not that the species or genus or dignity of the form are unattractive, but rather that the distribution is complicated and inconvenient in the arrangement of the triglyphs and ceiling work. 2. namque necesse est triglyphos constitui contra medios tetrantes columnarum, metopasque quae inter triglyphos fient aeque longas esse quam altas. contraque in angulares columnas triglyphi in extremis partibus constituuntur et non contra medios tetrantes. ita metopae, quae proximae ad angulares triglyphos fiunt, non exeunt quadratae sed oblongio

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 4.3 (angular triglyph). On the angular-triglyph problem, Gros's Budé (1992) devotes an extended commentary to the 'errors' that exegetes charge against Vitruvius, seeking to understand the logic of his choices rather than to correct them, and sets the passage within Vitruvius's polemic against the partisans of the Ionic order. Granger (Loeb) renders mendosum literally; Rowland and Howe explain the Roman half-metope solution with diagrams; Corso-Romano detail the terminology of tetrantes and metopae. This edition keeps the transmitted Latin (namque necesse est… est mendosum) unemended and translates in its own voice. The testimony of H and of the codices collated by Gros offers no variant here that alters the sense: the difficulty is doctrinal, not textual. 529

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 4.7 (Tuscan temple). The description of the Tuscan temple is collated with Gros's Budé (1992), which illuminates the passage with the evidence on Italo-Etruscan temples and the plan of the archaic Capitol; Gros stresses the tension between the Greek modular norm and the Italic practice that Vitruvius seeks to reconcile. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland– Howe (Cambridge, 1999) note that this chapter is the sole ancient source for the 'Tuscan order' that Serlio (1537) and Palladio (1570) would later codify; Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary (columen, mutuli, antepagmenta). This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense here. Editorial note. — Chapter 7 preserves the only ancient description of the Tuscan (Etruscan) temple, the native Italic type. Its proportions are broad and low: a plan nearly square, columns widely spaced and unfluted on simple bases (spirae), deep projecting eaves, and an entablature of timber rather than stone, crowned with terracotta ornaments. The plan is commonly divided to give three cellae — the arrangement of the great Capitoline temple of Jupiter, Juno and 547

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — IV.8. Monopteros, peripteros, tholos, pteroma and pseudoperipterum are distinct typological terms. The chapter assembles circular and hybrid arrangements rather than a single evolutionary sequence. The examples of Castor, Vediovis and Diana are Vitruvius’s exempla; modern identifications require separate documentation. His concluding uti mihi traditae sunt is methodologically significant: he presents principles as received, and differences may reflect the technical traditions available to him. 551

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Book IV. The running Latin is checked against Krohn (1912), with the authorial Spanish translation controlling the English interpretation. Supplements, seclusions, alternative printed readings and the transmitted text retain distinct status. In IV.7 the full sequence of five sections must be preserved; IV.8 distinguishes monopteral, peripteral and pseudoperipteral arrangements; IV.9 reads Vestae Terrae Matrique. Historical explanations of the orders are attributed to Vitruvius and distinguished from modern archaeological reconstruction. 1. Altars should face east and always stand below the cult images within the temple, so that those who pray and sacrifice look upward towards the deity. Their heights should vary according to the decor appropriate to each god. For Jupiter and all the celestial gods, make the altars as high as possible; for Vesta, Earth and the Mother, set them low. These principles yield altar forms appropriate in their proportions. Explanatory note — Bk. 4.9 (orientation of altars). The brief closing chapter of Book IV fixes the decorum of altars: they should face east and stand lower than the image of the god, so that the worshipper looks upward to the divinity. Vitruvius grades their height by the celestial hierarchy —very high for Jupiter and the gods of heaven; low for Vesta, Earth, and Sea (the chthonic and hearth deities)— applying to ritua

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — V, preface. Brevitas is an argument about transmitting specialized knowledge to a reader with limited time. The cube comparison supports measured and manageable writing; it is not merely incidental ornament. Technical terms that organize architectural concepts remain visible 158Vitruvius discusses six as a perfect number in Book III, chapter 1, and invokes the Pythagorean cube of six, 216, in the preface to Book V. The two passages concern different parts of his argument: bodily and numerical proportion in the former, the measured organization of technical writing in the latter. 557

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — Bk. 5.1.6–10 (Basilica at Fano). This is the only building Vitruvius declares he himself designed and superintended (conlocavi curavique), in the Colonia Iulia Fanestris (Fano). The passage was corrupt and is here restored after Rose: in 5.1.10, 'tecti nata dispositio' (not 'T uti notae'); in 563

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.1.6–10 (Basilica at Fano). In the Budé series, Book V is the work of Catherine Saliou (Les Belles Lettres, 2009), the volume that completes the collection and argues each difficult reading, weighing the alternatives before deciding; her commentary on the forensic basilica is fundamental. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) transmit the 'T-shaped' description which, as the critical note observes, derives from the corruption T uti notae; Tavernor and Schofield (Penguin, 2009) accompany their version with reconstructions. This edition restores the text after Rose and translates in its own voice. What is new with respect to the whole editorial tradition is the comparison with the archaeological discovery at Fano (2026), treated as preliminary evidence: for the first time the Vitruvian measurements (a testudo of 120×60 feet, columns of 50 feet) can be checked against material remains; see Appendix S. Editorial note. — In 5.1.6–10 Vitruvius describes the basilica he himself designed and supervised at the Colonia Iulia Fanestris (modern Fano) — the one building he explicitly claims as his own work (conlocavi curavique). He departs from the usual plan: the columns rise the full height of the hall (testudo), the aisle running round them; the tribunal is set in a hemicycle forty-six feet across; and a double arrangement of pediments crowns roof and

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — V.3. The theater’s healthy site, avoidance of southern exposure and cavea slope belong to Vitruvius’s environmental and medical framework. He distinguishes the horizontal and upward propagation of vox and seeks to avoid obstructions that impair intelligibility. A modern account of waves or the acoustic field remains commentary rather than a replacement for his ancient explanation. 570

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.6–5.7 (plan of the theater). The geometrical setting-out of the theater is one of the most studied passages of Book V. Catherine Saliou's Budé (2009) weighs the alternatives of restitution cautiously and warns that the Vitruvian scheme —four equilateral triangles inscribed in 581

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.7 (the Greek theater). Unlike the Roman theater—set out with four triangles (5.6)—the Greek is ordered with three squares inscribed in the circle of the orchestra. Hence its distinctive features: a wider orchestra, used by the chorus; a more recessed stage; and a platform (logeîon, λογεῖον) narrower and higher, of ten to twelve feet, since the actors perform on the proscaenium while the chorus moves below. The editions keep the Greek terminology; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) specify the reconstruction of the platform; Gros (Budé) relates it to the surviving Hellenistic theaters. The present edition keeps the Graecisms and translates in its own words. [Historical-architectural note] The Roman/Greek distinction reflects different scenic uses: at Rome, senators in the orchestra and the show on the pulpitum; in Greece, the chorus in the orchestra. In Greek theaters, not everything should be done according to the same principles, because first, in the lower circle, as in the Latin trigon IV, the squares of the three corners touch the line of the circle, and the side of the plaza that is next to the stage and cuts the curvature of the circle, in that region, the end of the proscenium is designated. And from that region to the end of the circle, a line parallel to the curvature is drawn, in which the front of the stage is formed, and through the center o

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.10 (baths). In the Budé, Book V is the work of Catherine Saliou (2009), whose commentary links the chapter with bath archaeology (Pompeii, Ostia) and with the improvement of the hypocaust attributed to Sergius Orata. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) fix the terminology (suspensura, hypocausis, praefurnium, testudo alvei, 600

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 5.12 (harbour works). Saliou's Budé (2009) comments on the chapter in the light of harbour archaeology; the passage is collated with 2.6 (where pozzolana is described) and with Strabo (5.4.6), Seneca, and Pliny, who confirm the Puteolan origin of the material. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) discuss the interpretation of Vitruvius's three methods, made difficult by the loss of the original diagrams. The decisive novelty is modern experimental verification: the ROMACONS project (Oleson, Hohlfelder, Brandon, Jackson; Building for Eternity, 2014) drilled ancient harbour concretes and cast a pila by the Vitruvian formula at Brindisi (2004), confirming its underwater set and a curing of about twelve months. This edition follows Rose's text and translates in its own voice. Then, at the designated place, the caisson (arca), framed with stout posts and chains, will be lowered into the water and firmly secured. The bottom between these blocks must then be leveled and cleaned underwater, and the rubble mixed with mortar, as described above, must be piled there until the space between the boxes is filled. This is the natural function of the places mentioned earlier. But if, due to waves or storms, the open ocean could not contain the planned arks, then a mattress should be built as firm as possible from the land or the shore itself, and the mattres

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Book V. The running Latin is checked against Krohn (1912). The preface’s reference to cubicis rationibus and CCXVI versus belongs to the organization of technical writing; the author’s wider cubic interpretation is developed separately in the preliminary study. Greek harmonic vocabulary is retained in the discussion of sound and sounding vessels. These checks do not constitute a new complete collation of the apparatuses of Rose, Granger or Budé. Editorial note. — Chapter 12 preserves the fullest ancient account of building in the sea. Where a natural harbour is wanting, Vitruvius describes a hydraulic mortar of lime and the volcanic ash of Puteoli (pulvis Puteolanus, pozzolana) that sets under water; it is poured within timber caissons (arcae) sunk and braced 614

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VI, preface. The philosophical and biographical exempla contrast fortune with disciplined education and support an ethical account of professional formation. They are part of Vitruvius’s moral self-presentation; rhetorical examples do not become independent biographical documentation merely because they occur in the preface. 623

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 6.1 (climate and the character of peoples). In the Budé, Book VI is the work of Louis Callebat (2004), whose commentary interweaves the passage with Ciceronian sources and with the Greek medical (the Hippocratic Airs, Waters, Places) and Aristotelian (Politics VII) tradition. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the background of climatic determinism and its Augustan reworking; Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary of the humours. This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text. The manuscript tradition (H, Harleianus 2767, and the codices collated by the Budé) offers no variant here that alters the sense: the interest of the passage is doctrinal and historical, not textual. Editorial note. — Vitruvius’s account of national character (6.1.3–11) belongs to the ancient theory of environmental determinism, descending from the Hippocratic treatise Airs, Waters, Places and from Aristotle’s Politics: climate was held to shape the body, temperament, and even the pitch of a people’s voice. The argument culminates, by convention, in praise of Italy’s central and temperate position as fitting Rome for empire — a topos of Augustan ideology. It is read today as a document of ancient ethnographic thought rather than as natural science. For the nations of Italy are the most temperate on both sides, and in the strength of their b

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 6.3. The terminology interpensiva, colliquiae, compluvium and impluvium should be compared with the technical discussions in Callebat’s Budé edition of Book VI (2004), Granger’s Loeb translation, Rowland and Howe (1999), and Corso and Romano (1997). This 639

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 6.7 (Greek house). In the Budé, Louis Callebat (2004) treats this chapter as a key witness to the Greco-Latin domestic vocabulary and discusses the terminological mismatches Vitruvius himself flags (andron, xystus, prothyrum/diathyron). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) recall that the Vitruvian account served as the basis for reconstructions of the Greek house before excavation, and that the finds at Delos, Priene, and Olynthus show plans more open and less rigid in the separation of the sexes than the text implies (as recent studies of the gynaeconitis and the andron, e.g. by S. Weir and H. Franks, have qualified). This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the Greek spelling of the technical terms; the gynaeconitis/andronitis division is presented as a Vitruvian category, not as secure archaeological fact. And to these are added larger houses that have more elaborate peristyles, in which there are four porticoes of equal height, or one facing south formed by taller columns. Now that peristyle, which has a taller portico, is called a Rhodo. And those houses have excellent vestibules and their own doors, with dignified porticoes and peristyles, decorated with wainscoting and roofing, and interior ceilings; large shutters with square doors, so that it can easily be spacious with four dining rooms, bedrooms, servants' quarters, and

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 6.8 (counterforts, anterides sive erismae). In the Budé, Book VI is the work of Louis Callebat (2004), who comments on the passage with the engineering of terraces and substructures. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) —whose plate labels it 'Retaining Walls and Buttresses (Anterides sive Erismae)'— stress Vitruvius's anticipation of the counterfort and of the distribution of thrust; Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (anterides, erismae, congestio). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice; H and the codices collated by the Budé offer no variant here that alters the sense. Therefore, to remedy this defect, it will be necessary to first determine the thickness of the structure in proportion to the mass of earth to be retained. Then, on the face, the buttresses (in Greek erismae) are built, set apart from one another by as much as the height of the future substructure, with the same thickness as the substructure; and it runs from below, for which the thickness of the substructure has been determined, then it gradually contracts, so that it has the greatest prominence, as much as the thickness of the work. 670

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Book VI. The running Latin is checked against Krohn (1912), and the authorial Spanish translation provides the basis for the English rendering. Climate, optical adjustment, domestic arrangements and structural stability belong to distinct stages of the book’s argument. Greek technical terms 673

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 7, preface. In the Budé, Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Marie-Thérèse Cam, and Michel Zuinghedau, whose commentary documents the sources of the catalog of authors and the Alexandrian anecdote. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the preface's value as an ancient testimony on plagiarism and on the Library of Alexandria; Corso–Romano clarify the Ptolemaic chronology (the anecdote conflates Ptolemy I with the earliest Ptolemies). This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense; the one uncertainty is historical —the exact identity of the king— not textual. 11. Igitur tales ingressus eorum quia ad propositi mei rationes animadverti praeparatos, inde sumendo progredi coepi. namque primum Agatharchus Athenis Aeschylo docente tragoediam scaenam fecit et de ea commentarium reliquit. ex eo moniti Democritus et Anaxagoras de eadem re scripserunt, quemadmodum oporteat ad aciem oculorum radiorumque extentionem certo loco centro constituto lineas ratione naturali respondere, uti de certa re certae imagines aedificiorum in scaenarum picturis redderent speciem et quae in directis planisque frontibus sint figurata, alia abscedentia, alia prominentia esse videantur. 11. Therefore, such were their entrances, because I observed that the reasons for my purpose were prepared, and I procee

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII, preface. The preface establishes the transmission of technical knowledge, condemns plagiarism and constructs a genealogy of writers on architecture, perspective and artistic theory. Its function in the treatise is substantive, not an expendable digression. The Aristophanes anecdote is read within that argument; ancient literary judgment and independently verified library history remain distinct. 684

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.2. Albarium opus denotes white lime finishing. Prolonged soaking and the test with an ascia are preserved as empirical checks on the lime’s 690

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.4. In damp places, sand, crushed pottery, the rough coat and finishing layers remain differentiated. Double walls, channels, cavities and moisture removal are ancient techniques. Expressions such as ‘vapor barrier’ may serve a clearly identified modern comparison, but should not replace the transmitted procedure or supply an unrecorded thickness. 700

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 7.5 (wall-painting). In the Budé, Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Marie-Thérèse Cam, and Michel Zuinghedau, whose commentary links the passage with Pompeian painting and the theory of decor. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) set it within the debate over the four Pompeian styles (Mau) and Vitruvius's relation to art criticism; Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary (monstra, tectoria, coliculi). Modern scholarship has debated whether Vitruvius is a reliable observer or a conservative moralist; this edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense. Editorial note. — This passage (7.5.3–4) is the locus classicus of ancient art criticism. Vitruvius condemns the fanciful wall-painting of the Third Pompeian Style — impossible architectures, hybrid figures, vegetal scrolls — as untruthful. When such Roman decoration was rediscovered underground (in “grottoes”) at 703

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.6. Marble for tectoria may denote powder or aggregate, not solid slabs. Crushing, grinding, sifting, application and polishing remain materially distinct. The supplement ⟨et cum⟩ articulates the sequence of grinding and subsequent sifting; its presence is editorially marked in the Latin even though the English renders the connection naturally. 707

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 7.8–7.9 (minium and quicksilver). In the Budé, Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Michel Zuinghedau, and Marie-Thérèse Cam (1995), whose commentary collates the passage with Theophrastus (De lapidibus 58), Pliny (Natural History 33.37–40), and Dioscorides (5.94). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the distinction, crucial for archaeometry, between Vitruvius's cinnabar (HgS) and red lead; Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (anthrax, hydrargyrum, ganosis). Modern physico-chemical analysis of Pompeian frescoes confirms both the use of cinnabar and its photochemical darkening —precisely the problem ganosis sought to prevent. This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. 4. ita obstans cerae ponticae lorica non patitur nec lunae splendorem nec solis radios lambendo eripere ex his politionibus colorem. quae autem in Ephesiorum metallis fuerunt officinae, nunc traiectae sunt ideo Romam quod id genus venae postea est inventum Hispaniae regionibus, e quibus metallis glaebae portantur et 713

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.10. Atramentum includes blacks obtained by different processes: soot from resin, charcoal from vine shoots or resinous timber, and calcined wine lees. Lacus, laconicum, fornacula, nares and glutinum are interpreted within the manufacturing apparatus. The similarity to indicum mentioned by Vitruvius concerns color and does not prove identity of material. 717

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 7.11 (Egyptian blue). The Budé of Liou, Zuinghedau, and Cam (1995) comments on the recipe in the light of the pigment's archaeometry; Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress that it is the only ancient textual source on its manufacture. Corso– 718

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.12. Cerussa, aeruca and sandaraca do not map invariably onto single modern substances. White lead prepared from lead and vinegar fumes is distinguished from the copper-associated aeruca, and sandaraca made by heating cerussa from the mineral sandaraca mentioned elsewhere. Translation should preserve those differences rather than harmonize the names. 720

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.13. Ostrum can refer to the dye-producing material, the mollusc or the color. Retaining the ancient term beside ‘purple’ helps preserve this range. The supplement ⟨rerum⟩ remains editorially visible. The geographical variation of color belongs to Vitruvius’s natural history, not a modern biological taxonomy. 722

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VII.14. Substitution colors made from rubia, hysginum, violets, vaccinium, luteum and other materials reveal an economy of architectural finishing. Ancient plant names remain where botanical identification is uncertain. The supplement ⟨ita⟩ is marked, and the historical practice of imitation is distinguished from a modern legal or commercial category of forgery. 724

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VIII, preface. The accounts of Thales, Heraclitus, the Magian priests, Euripides and Anaxagoras, and Egyptian tradition form an ancient philosophical frame for the discussion of water. Attributed doctrine, the history of philosophy and modern physical explanation are kept separate, without retrospectively harmonizing Vitruvius’s doxography. 727

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VIII.1. Water prospecting combines topographical, botanical and atmospheric signs. Creta, sabulo, glarea and saxum are translated according to their function in the passage without imposing excessively precise modern geological classifications. The excavation-test supplement ⟨tres, altus pedes⟩ remains visible as an editorial intervention. 732

entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — VIII.3.22–23. Krohn (1912, 185–186) prints these epigrams in Greek with conjectural supplements. The supplied words and lines retain angle brackets in the Greek text. Αὐτῆμαρ means ‘on that same day’; the statement concerns the loss of teeth, not brushing them. The epigrams express the ancient account of the springs’ supposed effects and are presented as historical testimony. [24] Sunt etiam nonnullis locis fontium proprietates, quae procreant qui ibi nascuntur egregiis vocibus ad cantandum, uti Tarso, Magnesiae, aliis eiusmodi regionibus. Etiamque Zama est civitas Afrorum, cuius moenia rex Iuba duplici muro saepsit ibique regiam domum sibi constituit. Ab ea milia passus XX est oppidum Ismuc, cuius agrorum regiones incredibili finitae sunt terminatione. Cum esset enim Africa parens et nutrix ferarum bestiarum, maxime serpentium, in eius agris oppidi nulla nascitur, et si quando adlata ibi ponatur, statim moritur; neque id solum, sed etiam terra ex his locis si alio translata fuerit, et ibi. Id genus terrae etiam Balearibus dicitur esse. Sed aliam mirabiliorem virtutem ea habet terra, quam ego sic accepi. 24. In some places the properties of springs are also said to give those born there exceptionally fine singing voices, as at Tarsus, Magnesia and similar regions. Zama is an African city which King Juba enclosed with a double wall and made 750

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VIII.3. Hot, mineral, brackish and extraordinary waters require a distinction between observed phenomena, ancient explanation and modern identification. Sulphur, alumen, bitumen and other material names remain visible. Therapeutic properties are attributed to Vitruvius and ancient medicine. Greek epigrams are treated as transmitted or editorially constituted texts; their verse divisions and uncertainties must not be lost in a prose transcription. 753

entries.label: Critical note
entries.text: Critical note — VIII.4. Expertiones and probationes denote empirical tests: the inhabitants’ condition, marks in bronze vessels, residue after boiling, the 754

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 8.5–8.6 (leveling and gradient). In the Budé, Book VIII is the work of Louis Callebat (1973), whose commentary reconstructs the chorobates and discusses its real precision. A. T. Hodge (Roman Aqueducts and Water Supply, 1992) argued that the chorobates was in truth a builder's level, not a surveyor's instrument capable of the very fine gradients (down to 1:20,000) of some aqueducts, and that Vitruvius misunderstood his Greek source. A point for the apparatus: all manuscripts of Vitruvius read semipede (half a foot per hundred), against the sicilici of Pliny's —a famous discrepancy between the two authors, not an internal variant. Granger (Loeb), Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999), and Corso–Romano collate the technical vocabulary (perpendiculum, canalis, libramentum). This edition keeps semipede with the tradition and translates in its own voice. Critical and instrumental note — VIII.5. The chorobates is an approximately twenty-foot leveling instrument using plumb lines and an upper water channel when wind interferes. Dioptra, libra aquaria, perpendiculum, norma and fastigium retain their technical identities. The discussion of the water surface and the spherical Earth is attributed to ancient physics and Vitruvius’s reference to Archimedes; it is not silently replaced with a modern surveyor’s specification. 758

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 8.6 (lead and health). Callebat's Budé (1973) comments on the passage alongside Pliny (Natural History 31.57-58 and 34.164) and Frontinus (De aquaeductu), who likewise treat the fistulae and the plumbarii. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress Vitruvius's lucidity and its limit (despite the warning, he went on designing conduits with lead). A. T. Hodge's study ('Vitruvius, Lead Pipes and Lead Poisoning,' American Journal of Archaeology, 1981) qualified the real extent of the risk (continuous flow, protective calcareous scale); recent archaeometry (Delile et al., PNAS, 2014) measured in the Tiber sediments lead up to a hundred times that of the springs. This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. entries.label: Textual note
entries.text: Textual note — Book VIII. The Latin is checked against Krohn (1912), with the Spanish authorial interpretation guiding the English. The argument distinguishes the search for water, its supposed natural properties, empirical tests, leveling and the construction of conduits. Ancient explanations of salubrity and therapeutic effects are preserved as historical claims. Uncertain gradients and pipe dimensions are not silently replaced with a single modern engineering specification. What I knew about the power and variety of water, and what advantages it has, and by what means it can all be extracted and tested, I have put in this volume; Next I will write about the gnomonic questions of clocks. Critical and engineering note — VIII.6. The text distinguishes constructed channels, lead pipes and earthenware tubes. The opening gradient is textually difficult, especially around sicilicus and differently supplied words. The apparatus retains the ancient reading instead of fabricating a uniquely certain metric slope. Pipe sizes, distribution, pressure effects and the relation between level and fall require separate consideration; a plausible hydraulic reconstruction does not, by itself, establish a manuscript reading. 767

entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 9, preface (the Pythagorean triangle). In the Budé, Book IX is the work of Jean Soubiran (1969). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress that Vitruvius describes the 3-4-5 right triangle, not the general proof of the theorem (Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics, I, 1921); the attribution to Pythagoras is traditional and disputed, since Pythagorean triples already appear on the Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 (c. 1800 BCE). On the sacrifice, the tradition (Cicero, Diogenes Laertius, Plutarch) wavers between the hecatomb of oxen and skepticism, given Pythagorean vegetarianism. Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (norma, trigonum). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. Likewise, Pythagoras shows that the rule was found without the invention of craftsmen, and how with much labor the craftsmen who make it can hardly keep it true. For if three rules are taken, one of which measures 3 feet, another 4 feet, and the third 5 feet, and these rules, combined together, touch, having at their ends the shape of a triangle, they distort the corrected standard. And for these regular lengths, if each square is described with equal sides, when it has three sides, the area will be 81 feet, which will be 44, 16, which will be 5, and 25. entries.label: Comparative note
entries.text: Comparative note — Bk. 9, preface (Hiero's crown). In the Budé, Book IX is the work of Jean Soubiran (1969), whose astronomical and mathematical commentary is standard. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress that the anecdote does not appear in Archimedes's surviving works (On Floating Bodies sets out the principle, not the episode) and that its technical plausibility has been questioned: the precision required by mere immersion is difficult, so it has been proposed that Archimedes in fact used hydrostatic weighing —a hypothesis already framed by Galileo in La Bilancetta (1586) and revisited by modern scholarship (Ch. Rorres). Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (massa, coronarium opus). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense.
